subject: English
topic: Sentence Improvement — grammatical corrections, style enhancement

questions.text: Improve: 'The student studied hard and he passed the exam.' Sentence suffix 'successfully' should be placed where?

options.option_text: 'The student studied hard successfully and he passed the exam.'
'The student studied hard and he successfully passed the exam.'
'Successfully the student studied hard and he passed the exam.'
'The student studied successfully hard and he passed the exam.'

questions.explanation: Adverb placement: 'successfully' modifies 'passed'. Place before main verb or after auxiliary. Best: 'he successfully passed' (option B). Trap: A (awkward), C (dangling), D (breaks verb-adverb).

questions.text: Improve: 'The benefits of exercise includes better health and more energy.' Identify error.

options.option_text: Change 'includes' to 'include' (plural subject 'benefits')
Change 'benefits' to 'benefit'
Change 'better' to 'best'
No error

questions.explanation: 'Benefits' is plural, requires plural verb 'include'. Correct: 'The benefits of exercise include better health...' Answer: A. Trap: mistaking 'exercise' as subject (it's object of preposition).

questions.text: Improve: 'He is one of the few students who has scored 95%.' Identify issue.

options.option_text: Change 'has' to 'have' (relative pronoun 'who' refers to plural 'students')
No error; 'has' is correct
Change 'is' to 'are'
Change 'scored' to 'scoring'

questions.explanation: 'Who' is relative pronoun referring to antecedent 'students' (plural). Verb in relative clause should be plural: 'have'. Correct: 'He is one of the few students who have scored 95%.' Answer: A. Trap: treating 'one' as subject of relative clause (it's not).

questions.text: Improve: 'Being a rainy day, we stayed home.' Issue?

options.option_text: Use 'Since it was a rainy day' (fix dangling participle)
Change 'stayed' to 'had stayed'
No error
Change 'day' to 'days'

questions.explanation: Dangling participle: 'Being a rainy day' doesn't properly modify 'we'. Subject of participle phrase should be clear. Correct: 'Since it was a rainy day, we stayed home' or 'Because it was raining, we stayed home.' Answer: A. Trap: accepting dangling modifier as acceptable.

questions.text: Improve: 'The report was written with accurate information and clearly.' Style issue?

options.option_text: 'The report was written with accurate information and clarity.' (parallel nouns)
'The report was written accurately and clearly.' (parallel adverbs)
No error
'The report was clear and written accurately.'

questions.explanation: Parallel structure: mix of noun 'information' and adverb 'clearly' is non-parallel. Option B maintains parallel adverbs: 'accurately and clearly'. Answer: B. Trap: A (still mixed), D (different structure).

questions.text: Improve: 'Neither the manager or the employees were satisfied.' Error?

options.option_text: Change 'or' to 'nor' (neither...nor structure)
Change 'were' to 'was'
No error
Change 'Neither' to 'Both'

questions.explanation: Correlative conjunction: 'neither...or' is incorrect. Use 'neither...nor'. Correct: 'Neither the manager nor the employees were satisfied.' Answer: A. Trap: confusing correlative pair structures.

questions.text: Improve: 'Having completed the project on time, the team was praised for their efficiency.' Issue?

options.option_text: No error; clear participle modification
Change 'was praised' to 'have been praised'
Change 'their' to 'its'
Change 'efficiency' to 'efficient'

questions.explanation: Participle phrase 'Having completed the project on time' clearly modifies subject 'the team'. No dangling modifier. Verb tense shift is acceptable. Answer: A. Trap: assuming all participial phrases at the beginning are dangling (they're not if subject is clear).

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly improves the sentence: 'The new smartphone model is more superior to its predecessor in overall performance'?

options.option_text: The new model is superior than its predecessor in overall performance
The new model is most superior to its predecessor in overall performance
The new model is superior to its predecessor in overall performance
The new model is more superior than its predecessor in overall performance

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'superior' is itself a comparative adjective (from Latin 'superus'), so adding 'more' creates a double comparative — a clear grammatical error. The correct preposition with 'superior' is always 'to', never 'than'. Option A corrects the redundancy but introduces the wrong preposition 'than', making it incorrect. Option B wrongly uses the superlative 'most'. Option D compounds both errors.

questions.stem: Select the correct improvement for the sentence: 'My grandfather has been living in this city since thirty years'.

options.option_text: My grandfather has been living in this city from thirty years
My grandfather has been living in this city for thirty years
My grandfather had been living in this city since thirty years
My grandfather was living in this city since thirty years ago

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'for' is used with a period or duration of time (thirty years = a span), whereas 'since' is used with a specific point in time (since 2005, since Monday). The present perfect continuous 'has been living' correctly signals an action that started in the past and continues now. Option A wrongly uses 'from', which requires a corresponding 'to'. Option C incorrectly shifts to past perfect. Option D awkwardly pairs 'since' with 'years ago'.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct improvement for the sentence: 'If I was in his position, I would resign from the committee immediately'?

options.option_text: If I were in his position, I would resign from the committee immediately
If I was in his position, I should resign from the committee immediately
If I were in his position, I should have resigned from the committee immediately
Were I in his position, I would have resigned from the committee immediately

questions.explanation: A is correct because hypothetical or unreal present conditions require the subjunctive mood, which uses 'were' for all persons — including first person singular. 'If I was' uses the indicative past and is grammatically wrong in a hypothetical context. Option B retains the error 'was' and incorrectly substitutes 'should' for 'would'. Option C fixes 'were' but wrongly shifts the result clause to past perfect ('should have resigned'), implying a past missed action rather than a present hypothetical. Option D (formal inversion) also shifts the result to past perfect, changing the meaning.

questions.stem: Identify the correct improvement for: 'The committee decided to revert back to the original proposal after extensive discussions'.

options.option_text: The committee decided to return back to the original proposal after extensive discussions
The committee decided to revert to the original proposal after extensive discussions
The committee decided to revert back on the original proposal after extensive discussions
The committee decided to revert again to the original proposal after extensive discussions

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'revert' already means 'to go back to a previous state', making 'back' entirely redundant — a classic tautology error commonly tested in SSC/IBPS exams. Option A is equally wrong because 'return back' carries the same redundancy ('return' already implies coming back). Option C uses the wrong preposition 'on' after 'revert'. Option D replaces 'back' with 'again', which is a subtler but still redundant addition since reverting implies a return.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly improves: 'The helpline received less complaints after the revised guidelines were published'?

options.option_text: The helpline received fewer complaints after the revised guidelines were published
The helpline received lesser complaints after the revised guidelines were published
The helpline had received less complaint after the revised guidelines were published
The helpline received fewest complaints after the revised guidelines were published

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'fewer' is used with countable nouns and 'complaints' is countable (you can count individual complaints). 'Less' is reserved for uncountable or mass nouns such as water, time, or information. Option B uses 'lesser', which functions as an adjective meaning 'of lower importance' (e.g., the lesser evil) and cannot modify countable quantities. Option C wrongly makes 'complaint' singular and shifts to past perfect without cause. Option D uses the superlative 'fewest', which would imply comparison with multiple other periods, a meaning not supported by the context.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly improves the sentence: 'The reason for the project delay is because the shipment was held at customs'?

options.option_text: The reason for the delay is due to the fact that shipment was held at customs
The reason for the project delay is that the shipment was held at customs
The reason of the project delay is because the shipment was held at customs
The reason behind the project delay is since the shipment was held at customs

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'The reason is because' is a circular, redundant construction — 'reason' and 'because' both express causation, creating a logical repetition. The standard rule, rigorously enforced in formal English and competitive exams, is to use 'The reason is that...' Option A avoids 'because' but replaces it with the equally verbose 'due to the fact that', which fails the conciseness test and also drops the article before 'shipment'. Option C keeps the original 'because' error and compounds it with the wrong preposition 'of' after 'reason' (correct: 'reason for'). Option D replaces 'because' with 'since', which still functions causally and reproduces the same redundancy.

questions.stem: Identify the correctly improved version of: 'Hardly he had entered the examination hall when the invigilator announced a change in seating'.

options.option_text: Hardly had he entered the examination hall when the invigilator announced a change in seating
Hardly had he entered the examination hall than the invigilator announced a change in seating
Hardly he entered the examination hall when the invigilator announced a change in seating
Scarcely had he entered the examination hall before the invigilator announced a change in seating

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'Hardly' is a negative adverb, and when placed at the front of a clause it triggers subject-auxiliary inversion: 'Hardly + had + subject + V3'. The correlating conjunction for 'hardly/scarcely' is 'when', never 'than' (which is paired exclusively with 'No sooner'). Option B correctly applies inversion but wrongly uses 'than' — a very common error because candidates confuse this pattern with 'No sooner...than'. Option C omits the mandatory inversion entirely. Option D applies correct inversion with 'scarcely' but pairs it with 'before', which is non-standard; the accepted pairing is 'scarcely...when'. Both errors in B and D are frequent exam traps.

questions.stem: Which option best replaces the underlined part in the sentence: 'The new traffic regulations have resulted in less accidents on the highway'?

options.option_text: fewer accidents on the highway
lesser accidents on the highway
least accidents on the highway
less number of accidents on the highway

questions.explanation: 'Fewer' is correct because 'accidents' is a countable noun; 'less' is used only with uncountable nouns (e.g., 'less water'). 'Lesser' is an adjective meaning 'smaller in importance or size', not a quantity word for countables. Option D is redundant — 'number of accidents' would need 'fewer number', but even then the phrasing is awkward.

questions.stem: Which correction is needed in the sentence: 'She worked as a district judge since 2012 and is still serving in the same post'?

options.option_text: was working as a district judge since 2012
has worked as a district judge since 2012
had been working as a district judge since 2012
worked as a district judge starting from 2012

questions.explanation: When an action began in the past and continues to the present, the present perfect tense must be used with 'since'. 'Has worked' correctly signals this unbroken continuation. 'Had been working' (option C) implies the action ended before another past event — contradicted here by 'is still serving'. Simple past 'worked' (option D) severs the link to the present that 'since' demands.

questions.stem: Which option correctly improves the sentence: 'The accused denied that he had not received the stolen property'?

options.option_text: denied that he had received the stolen property
denied not having received any stolen property
denied that he had never received the stolen property
denied the fact that he had not received the stolen property

questions.explanation: The original sentence contains a double negative: 'denied' (= said it was false) combined with 'had not received' logically asserts he DID receive the property — the opposite of the intended meaning. Removing the inner negation ('had received') corrects this. Option B ('denied not having') still creates a double negative: deny + not = affirmation. Option C adds 'never', another negation that recreates the same logical error.

questions.stem: Which revision removes the ambiguity caused by the misplaced word 'only' in the sentence: 'The auditor only reviewed the files that were flagged for irregularities'?

options.option_text: The auditor reviewed only the files that were flagged for irregularities
Only the auditor reviewed the files that were flagged for irregularities
The auditor reviewed the files only that were flagged for irregularities
The auditor reviewed the files that only were flagged for irregularities

questions.explanation: Placing 'only' immediately before the element it restricts removes ambiguity. The intended meaning is a restriction on WHAT was reviewed, so 'only' must precede 'the files'. In the original, 'only reviewed' modifies the verb, suggesting the auditor did nothing except review (a weak and ambiguous reading). Option B shifts meaning to WHO reviewed, not what. Options C and D create syntactically awkward or wrong constructions.

questions.stem: Identify the correction needed in the sentence: 'If the principal was stricter, fewer students would bunk classes'?

options.option_text: If the principal is stricter, fewer students would bunk classes
If the principal were stricter, fewer students would bunk classes
If the principal had been stricter, fewer students would bunk classes
If the principal would be stricter, fewer students would bunk classes

questions.explanation: A present unreal (hypothetical) conditional requires the subjunctive mood: 'were' for all persons, including third-person singular. 'Was' (indicative past) is grammatically non-standard here. Option C ('had been') shifts to a past unreal conditional, changing the sentence to mean the condition could never be fulfilled — an unintended meaning. Option D is incorrect because 'would be' must never appear in the if-clause of a conditional.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly structured replacement for the underlined part in: 'No sooner had the candidate submitted the form when the portal closed'?

options.option_text: No sooner did the candidate submit the form when the portal closed
No sooner the candidate had submitted the form than the portal closed
No sooner had the candidate submitted the form than the portal closed
No sooner had the candidate submitted the form before the portal closed

questions.explanation: The correlative conjunction 'no sooner' must be paired with 'than', not 'when' or 'before'. The structure also demands subject-auxiliary inversion after 'no sooner' at the start of a clause — hence 'had the candidate submitted' (not 'the candidate had submitted'). Option A retains the inversion but uses 'when' (wrong correlative). Option B drops the inversion (wrong). Option D uses 'before', which pairs with 'hardly/scarcely', not 'no sooner'.

questions.stem: Which option is the correct reported speech version of the sentence: 'She said, I will resign if they do not increase my salary'?

options.option_text: She said that she will resign if they do not increase her salary
She said that she would resign if they did not increase her salary
She said that she would resign if they do not increase her salary
She said that she would resign if they would not increase her salary

questions.explanation: When the reporting verb ('said') is in the past tense, backshift applies: 'will' → 'would' and 'do not' → 'did not'. Both shifts must occur consistently. Option A applies no backshift at all. Option C shifts 'will' to 'would' but leaves 'do not' unchanged — a common half-shift error. Option D incorrectly uses 'would not' in the if-clause; in reported conditionals the if-clause takes simple past ('did not'), never 'would'.
